title: Federal District Court Denies Fed’s Request to Pause Yellowstone Bison Lawsuit
author: Mike Garrity
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/American_bison_k5680-1.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/23/federal-
district-court-denies-feds-request-to-pause-yellowstone-bison-lawsuit/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/American_bison_k5680-1.jpg)

American Bison. Photo: Jack Dykinga, Agricultural Research Service, US
Department of Agriculture. Public Domain.

The federal district court in Montana denied the federal government’s request
to press pause on a lawsuit challenging the way that the federal government is
managing the American Bison (the National Mammal) in Yellowstone National Park
on July 21st. The lawsuit, filed by conservation groups Alliance for the Wild
Rockies and Council on Wildlife and Fish, challenges the government’s failure
to use the best available science in wildlife management of the National
Mammal.

In response to the lawsuit, the federal government asked the court to
indefinitely pause the lawsuit while the government conducts additional
analysis. However, the court rejected the request to pause the case, finding
in part that the government had not made any commitment to address the
problems raised in the lawsuit. Additionally, pausing the lawsuit would harm
the public interest because wild bison would continue to be managed under a
plan that does not apply the best available science, whereas if the case
continues on time then the court could issue an order that would require
better management.

This court decision is a great step in the right direction — we need to base
the management of our National Mammal on sound science. This is the purpose of
this lawsuit, and we are happy to report that the lawsuit will continue as
planned. We already filed our first brief on July 1, and our arguments are
strong for our wild, free-roaming bison.

For context, tens of millions of wild bison once roamed across western North
America. Today, wild bison occupy less than one percent of their former range.
Despite their small population, every year, the federal government rounds up
and slaughters wild roaming bison that try to migrate outside Yellowstone
National Park. The original reason for this wildlife management action was a
fear that wild bison would transmit a disease called brucellosis to domestic
cattle that might be grazing outside the National Park. In the 1990s, little
was known regarding brucellosis transmission to cattle, and so the original
government management plan for brucellosis, issued in 2000, focused solely on
wild bison — keeping them separate from cattle and slaughtering bison that
tested positive for brucellosis antibodies.

However, after 20 years of management under the prior bison management plan,
the federal government commissioned the National Academies of Science,
Medicine, and Engineering to undertake an exhaustive study to determine if
brucellosis management was working in the Yellowstone region. Contrary to the
original assumptions in the 2000 plan, the National Academies found that over
the past 20 years, wild elk — not wild bison — transmitted brucellosis to
livestock 27 times. Wild bison were not responsible for a single transmission.

Then, in 2024, the federal government prepared and approved a new management
plan for wild bison. Yet, like an ostrich with its head stuck in the sand, the
government completely ignored the National Academies' recommendations to
switch focus from wild bison to wild elk for brucellosis management in the
Greater Yellowstone Area. Not a single alternative in the new plan’s EIS
addresses the true source of brucellosis infections — elk.

Therefore we had to sue because no one else would hold the federal
government’s feet to the fire. There is no scientific dispute here, the bison
management plan is based on outdated assumptions that thousands of bison need
to be slaughtered to stop brucellosis infections in cattle. This is no longer
accepted science and the government needs to change its management practices
to keep up and base its decisions on the best available science.

Additionally, the government failed to show the public where (if at all) wild
bison might actually overlap with active cattle grazing allotments during a
time of year when cattle are present and brucellosis is a risk. Without this
basic information, it’s impossible to know where cattle might interact with
brucellosis-infected fetal tissue from wild bison, and so we don’t know where
or if these aggressive management practices are needed at all to keep cattle
separate from wild bison. Over the past three decades, cattle grazing has
diminished in this area, and so things just aren’t the same now as they were
in the 1990’s when the original plan was created.

Furthermore, after 21 years of implementation, the most aggressive and
controversial tool in the management plan — 'capture and slaughter’ — has
failed to reduce the percentage of Yellowstone bison that annually test
positive for brucellosis antibodies. The Bison Management Plan's Environmental
Impact Statement provides no rational reason to continue this aggressive and
controversial tool when it has proven to be ineffective at its sole purpose:
reducing brucellosis.

To be clear, when they test bison, they are testing bison to see if they have
been exposed to brucellosis. They are not testing to see if bison have been
infected with brucellosis or not.

The court allowed our lawsuit to continue and thus we need your help. Please
consider [donating to the Alliance for the Wild Rockies to help us fight for
wild bison](https://allianceforthewildrockies.org/take-action/). Please also
consider [donating to Counterpunch](https://www.counterpunch.org/donations/)
so they can continue to keep the public informed about the actions of our
government.
